findings.lens: charismatic non-denominational (Vineyard, Bethel, Hillsong, Third Wave)
findings.claim: The covenantal pole is written as amillennial ('with his return bringing the new creation'), so historic premillennialism, the Vineyard's actual position and the view named in history[4], has no home on the axis.
findings.evidence: fair_summary: 'Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation' versus 'a future earthly kingdom, usually preceded by the rapture'. Ladd (The Gospel of the Kingdom, 1959; The Blessed Hope, 1956): one people of God, kingdom present now, future earthly millennium, church through the tribulation. A Vineyard reader will see themselves in neither paragraph.
findings.fix: Append to the covenantal paragraph: 'Some on this side (historic premillennialists) still expect a future earthly reign of Christ, but with one people of God and the church passing through the tribulation.'

findings.claim: The fair summary assigns the inaugurated kingdom to the covenantal side and describes the covenantal side as amillennialism only; our side is described by its eschatology alone, with no hermeneutical principle.
findings.evidence: Quoted: "Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation" (covenantal half) and "The dispensational view keeps Israel and the church distinct: God's promises to national Israel will be fulfilled literally in a future earthly kingdom, usually preceded by the rapture of the church and a seven-year tribulation." The defining thesis of progressive dispensationalism, which the read-more list cites, is that the Davidic kingdom is already inaugurated with Christ enthroned (Blaising & Bock, Progressive Dispensationalism, 1993, chs. 6–7; Bock on Acts 2:30–36), so 'kingdom present now' as a covenantal marker excludes half our own camp. On the other side, covenant theology includes postmillennialists (Edwards, Hodge, Warfield) and historic premillennialists (Spurgeon, Horatius Bonar); 'return bringing the new creation' with no millennium is amillennialism, not covenant theology. The summary of our side never mentions the plain-sense hermeneutic (Ryrie's second sine qua non), which is what we would say the disagreement is about.
findings.fix: "The covenantal view sees one people of God across both testaments: the church, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, inherits the promises to Abraham, and the Old Testament is read in the light of its fulfilment in Christ. The dispensational view holds that Israel and the church are distinct in God's plan: the promises to national Israel, read in their plain sense, await fulfilment in Christ's earthly kingdom after his return, and the church is a distinct body that began at Pentecost. Most, though not all, dispensationalists also expect the church to be caught up before the tribulation, and progressive dispensationalists hold that Christ's kingdom has already begun."

findings.claim: 'Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation' defines the covenantal pole as amillennial. Historic premillennialists (Ladd, whom history:4 cites for 'one people of God') and postmillennialists are covenantal on the Israel/church question but expect a millennium.
findings.evidence: Ladd, The Blessed Hope (1956) and A Theology of the New Testament: one people of God, future millennium. WCF and the Reformed confessions leave the millennium open; Riddlebarger's amillennial book in read-more is one option within the pole, not the pole.
findings.fix: '...inherits the promises to Abraham, and Christ's kingdom is already present, whatever they expect of a future millennium.'

findings.lens: Pentecostal (Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths)
findings.claim: 'The dispensational view keeps Israel and the church distinct' is the defining clause, so the paragraph reads as if everyone at the right pole holds two peoples of God; Pentecostals hold the rapture, tribulation, millennium and salvation of national Israel while typically reading the church as the fulfilment of Joel's promise.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 14: 'This millennial reign will bring the salvation of national Israel (Ezekiel 37:21,22; Zephaniah 3:19,20; Romans 11:26,27) and the establishment of universal peace' -- salvation, not a separate programme. See also Sheppard, Pneuma 6 (1984).
findings.fix: After 'a seven-year tribulation.' add: 'Premillennial Pentecostals share this future hope for Israel and the pretribulational rapture without the full dispensational scheme.'

findings.lens: Presbyterian / Reformed (Westminster Standards, Three Forms of Unity)
findings.claim: The covenantal description omits the mechanism ('in Christ') and gives no room for the common Reformed expectation of a future conversion of ethnic Israel, so a Reformed reader who holds it may hesitate on S10.
findings.evidence: Galatians 3:16, 29; WLC 191; Murray, Romans 11:26; Hodge, Systematic Theology III.xx.4; the postmillennial wing (Bahnsen, Gentry, Mathison) also expects the kingdom to fill the earth before the return.
findings.fix: "The covenantal view sees one people of God across both testaments: in Christ, the church of Jew and Gentile together inherits the promises to Abraham; Christ's kingdom is present now and, for many, will yet see Israel's large-scale conversion, with his return bringing the new creation."

findings.claim: 'Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation' equates the covenantal pole with amillennialism, leaving covenantal historic-premillennialists and postmillennialists (both common among Reformed Baptists) without a home on their own side.
findings.evidence: Spurgeon and many 17th-century Particular Baptists (Knollys, Keach) were premillennial covenant theologians; the history line for Ladd concedes the position exists.
findings.fix: '...and Christ's kingdom is present now, whatever they hold about a future millennium, with his return bringing the new creation.'

findings.lens: Reformed charismatic (John Piper, Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms, Sovereign Grace Churches, Acts 29 continuationists)
findings.claim: The covenantal pole is described as amillennial only ('his return bringing the new creation') and, with history entry 1646 'covenant of works and the covenant of grace', as Westminster covenant theology, which excludes the historic premillennialists and Baptists who make up most of my tradition.
findings.evidence: Piper and Grudem (ST ch. 55) are historic premillennialists after Ladd, whom the history itself lists at 1950s; Bethlehem, Sovereign Grace and Acts 29 are Baptist bodies that do not hold a covenant of works, and progressive covenantalists (Gentry & Wellum) reject covenant theology as a system while holding one people of God. All of them score 15-30 on this axis and are told they are 'covenantal'.
findings.fix: ...the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham, and Christ's kingdom is present now; his return brings the new creation, for some after an earthly reign of Christ. Many Baptists who reject covenant theology as a system still stand on this side.

findings.claim: The covenantal summary describes amillennialism only ('Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation'), so a historic premillennialist who holds one people of God is told the left pole excludes a future millennium and the right pole excludes his ecclesiology.
findings.evidence: The history array itself (1950s, Ladd) says historic premillennialism holds 'a future millennium, one people of God', but neither summary paragraph contains that combination. It is the most common eschatology among SBC seminary faculty and is the view of Blomberg & Chung (eds.), A Case for Historic Premillennialism (2009).
findings.fix: '...and Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation (some, the historic premillennialists, expect a millennial reign first, but still with one people of God).'
